faqs.a: For general-population surveys, 385 responses at 95% confidence and 5% margin of error is the standard benchmark when the population is unknown or very large. If you know your population is small, enter it above and the correction will lower the number.
faqs.q: What is a good sample size for a survey?

faqs.a: 5% is the standard choice for most surveys. Use 3% when decisions are high-stakes and you can afford the much larger sample; use 10% only for quick exploratory polls where rough direction is enough.
faqs.q: What margin of error should I use?

faqs.a: The term p x (1 - p) in the formula — the variance — reaches its maximum at p = 0.5. Using 50% is the conservative, safest choice when you have no prior estimate of the true proportion.
faqs.q: Why does a 50% proportion give the biggest sample size?

faqs.a: Only when your sample would be more than about 5% of the total population. For populations above roughly 20,000 it changes almost nothing, so you can leave the population field blank.
faqs.q: When do I need the finite population correction?

faqs.a: You can, but your real margin of error grows — the results become less precise. It is better to collect the minimum shown, and to invite extra people to cover non-response.
faqs.q: Can I collect fewer responses than the calculator says?

faqs.a: No. A/B tests need a power calculator that accounts for baseline conversion rate and minimum detectable effect. This tool is designed for proportion-based surveys.
faqs.q: Does this work for A/B tests?

sample-size-calculator.formula:
n0 = Z^2 x p x (1 - p) / E^2
n = n0 / (1 + (n0 - 1) / N)   (finite-population correction)

Z = z-score for the confidence level, p = proportion, E = margin of error, N = population size.
Always round the result UP to the next whole respondent.
howTo: Choose your confidence level: 95% is the standard for most surveys, 99% for high-stakes research.
Enter your margin of error — 5% is typical; smaller values demand far more responses.
Enter the expected population proportion, or keep 50% when you have no prior estimate (it gives the safest result).
Optionally enter your total population size to apply the finite-population correction; leave it blank for unknown or very large populations.
Read the required sample size — that is the minimum number of complete responses to collect.
keyFacts: The classic research setup — 95% confidence with a 5% margin of error — needs 385 respondents for an unknown or very large population.
A 50% population proportion (p = 0.5) produces the largest and safest sample size; use it when you have no prior estimate.
Shrinking the margin of error from 5% to 3% roughly triples the required sample, because error sits in the denominator squared.
For small known populations the finite-population correction lowers the requirement: a population of 500 needs only 218 responses at 95% confidence and 5% error.
Z-scores used by this tool: 1.645 for 90%, 1.96 for 95%, and 2.576 for 99% confidence.

sample-size-calculator.workedExample:
95% confidence (Z = 1.96), 5% margin of error (E = 0.05), proportion 50% (p = 0.5), population unknown:
n0 = 1.96^2 x 0.5 x 0.5 / 0.05^2 = 3.8416 x 0.25 / 0.0025 = 0.9604 / 0.0025 = 384.16
Round UP: 385 respondents.

With a known population of 10,000:
n = 384.16 / (1 + 383.16 / 10000) = 384.16 / 1.038316 = 369.98
Round UP: 370 respondents.
